lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you met trade links. What is an import? (Something a country buys from another country.) Today: globalisation: how trade, travel and communication join the world together.

Globalisation means the world's places becoming more connected: goods, money, people, ideas and information moving faster and further. Your clothes, your phone and your breakfast may come from a dozen countries.

A country's exports are what it sells abroad; imports are what it buys. Exports minus imports is the trade balance: a surplus when exports are bigger, a deficit when imports are. Countries trade because each makes some things best.
Many products are made in a supply chain across countries. A T-shirt's cotton may be grown in one country and spun and woven in another. It may be sewn in a third and sold in a fourth.

About 80% of goods traded by weight go by sea. The steel shipping container (1956) made loading quick and cheap, and the biggest ships now carry over 20,000. Busy routes pass through the Suez and Panama Canals.

Undersea cables carry almost all internet traffic between continents, with satellites helping. Flights link cities in hours. Video calls and online shops let people work, learn and buy across the world.

Globalisation brings cheaper goods, jobs and new foods and ideas. But some workers lose jobs when factories move, some earn very little in poor conditions, and long journeys add pollution. Fair trade aims to pay farmers and workers fairly.
Try it in the world: trade with a friend's village. Find something each of you makes best, agree a fair swap, and follow your goods' journey. Next: energy for the world.

exercises.hint: 'Ex' means out: which way do the goods go?
exercises.explain: An export is something a country sells to other countries.

exercises.prompt: A country exports 500 million gold of goods and imports 420 million. What is its trade balance, in million gold?
exercises.hint: Take the imports from the exports.

exercises.prompt: About 80% of the goods traded by weight go by sea.
exercises.hint: Look back at the card about container ships.
exercises.explain: True: ships carry most of the world's goods by weight.

exercises.hint: Think of goods, people and ideas moving between places.
exercises.explain: The world's places becoming more connected by trade, travel and communication.

exercises.prompt: Put the making of a T-shirt in order.
items: it is sold in a shop
exercises.hint: Start in the field and end in the shop.
exercises.explain: Grown, spun, woven, sewn, then sold.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: goods, people or information on the move?
exercises.hint: What is actually travelling: things, people, or data?
exercises.explain: Goods: ships, a lorry of fruit. People: tourists, students. Information: video calls, emails.

exercises.prompt: A country imports 750 million gold of goods and exports 600 million. What is its deficit, in million gold?
exercises.hint: Take the smaller amount from the bigger one.

exercises.prompt: Match each link to what it carries.
exercises.explain: Cables: data. Ships: goods. Aeroplanes: people and post. Pipelines: oil and gas.

exercises.prompt: Why was the shipping container so important?
choices: it made loading quick and cheap
exercises.hint: Think how long loading a ship took box by box and sack by sack.
exercises.explain: Standard containers move straight from ship to train or lorry, so loading is fast and cheap.

exercises.prompt: Undersea cables carry almost all the internet's traffic between continents.
exercises.hint: Look back at the card about communication.
exercises.explain: True: satellites help, but cables carry almost all of it.

exercises.prompt: Which is a downside of globalisation for some people?
choices: jobs lost when factories move abroad
exercises.hint: Think of the workers in a town whose factory closes.
exercises.explain: When a factory moves to where costs are lower, the workers left behind can lose their jobs.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a benefit of globalisation, or a cost?
items: very low pay in some factories
exercises.hint: Who gains, and who loses, from each?
exercises.explain: Benefits: cheaper clothes, new jobs, foods from everywhere. Costs: pollution, very low pay, shops closing.

exercises.prompt: A ship carries 20,000 containers. A train takes 100 containers. How many trains would move the whole load?
exercises.hint: Divide the containers by what one train takes.

exercises.prompt: What does fair trade try to do?
choices: pay farmers and workers a fair price
exercises.hint: Think who grows the cocoa and coffee, and what they earn.
exercises.explain: It agrees a fair, steady price and decent conditions for farmers and workers.

exercises.prompt: Every country makes everything it needs by itself.
exercises.hint: Think of coffee in Britain or oil in Japan.
exercises.explain: False: countries trade because none can make everything well; they depend on each other.
